title: Managed LLM Platforms — Bedrock, Vertex AI, Azure OpenAI

questions.question: Before this lesson, which platform would you reach for first if a customer needed Claude, Llama, and Cohere behind one API?
options: AWS Bedrock, the marketplace bet that puts Claude, Llama, Titan, Cohere, and more behind one API and one IAM surface
Vertex AI, the Gemini-first bet that puts Google's own models ahead of the Model Garden third-party catalog and its 1M-token context
Azure OpenAI Service, the exclusive OpenAI partnership limited to GPT, DALL·E, and Whisper in the catalog
Direct Anthropic API, the single-vendor route with no marketplace, no PTUs, and no cross-model failover
questions.explanation: The lesson describes AWS Bedrock as the marketplace strategy: Claude, Llama, Titan, Stability, Cohere, and Mistral behind one API, one IAM surface, and one CloudWatch export.

questions.question: Which hyperscaler's bet is described as exclusive partnership rather than marketplace?
options: Vertex AI, betting on Gemini first with Model Garden as a secondary catalog
Azure OpenAI Service, betting only on OpenAI's own model family across GPT, DALL·E, and Whisper
AWS Bedrock, betting on breadth across Claude, Llama, Titan, Stability, Cohere, and Mistral in one marketplace
OCI Generative AI, a bet the lesson does not size up against the other three hyperscalers
questions.explanation: Azure OpenAI Service is described as an exclusive OpenAI partnership: only OpenAI models (GPT-4/4o/5/o-series, DALL-E, Whisper) are in the catalog, betting that OpenAI remains the frontier and customers want enterprise controls on that one relationship.

questions.question: Roughly what is the measured median TTFT gap between Azure OpenAI (with PTUs) and Bedrock on-demand on Llama 3.1 405B equivalents?
options: ~25 ms
~5 ms
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Artificial Analysis numbers: Azure OpenAI median TTFT around 50 ms (with PTUs) versus Bedrock on-demand around 75 ms, a gap of roughly 25 ms driven by dedicated versus shared capacity.

questions.question: Which Bedrock 2025 feature gives the cleanest per-product cost attribution natively in CloudWatch?
options: Bedrock Knowledge Bases, a retrieval-augmentation feature the lesson does not credit with any cost-attribution or CloudWatch-native role
Application Inference Profiles, added in 2025, tagged with team/product/feature so CloudWatch breaks out cost per profile natively
Bedrock Guardrails, a safety-filtering feature the lesson does not credit with any cost-attribution role
Bedrock Agents, an orchestration feature the lesson does not credit with any cost-attribution role
questions.explanation: The lesson names Application Inference Profiles, added in 2025, as the cleanest native attribution: tag a profile with team/product/feature and CloudWatch breaks out cost per profile without post-processing.

questions.question: Azure PTUs typically break even versus on-demand at what sustained utilization band?
questions.explanation: The lesson states PTUs are billed as a fixed hourly reservation regardless of traffic, and the break-even against on-demand pricing is usually around 40-60% sustained utilization.

questions.question: Why is the lesson's recommended 2026 policy a two-provider minimum for product-critical LLM calls?
options: Hyperscalers refuse to sign BAAs unless you also use a competitor, so a second vendor is needed just to get compliance sign-off
Frontier model leadership rotates monthly, so single-vendor lock-in shuts you out of two-thirds of the frontier
It is required by SOC 2 Type II, which audits refuse to certify for a single-vendor LLM deployment
Single-vendor pricing is always more expensive than splitting spend across two competing hyperscalers
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that because frontier leadership rotates monthly across providers, single-hyperscaler lock-in shuts a product out of two-thirds of the frontier, so a two-provider minimum (e.g. Bedrock plus Azure OpenAI) with gateway failover is the working pattern.
